extracted.intended_audience: reporters on the police beat; journalism students and editors responsible for crime coverage
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporting crime and police matters accurately, ethically, and usefully — covering sources (blotter, bureaus, confidential records), fairness to accused and victims, verification, and how to phrase operational details so as not to aid criminals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value versus harm of crime news
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime news can be of 'pinnacle social value or of abysmal social harm, depending upon how it is written.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of positive values: reveals the condition of law-enforcing agencies (honest/corrupt, alert/sleepy, shrewd/stupid), provides public check on police, prevents injustice by keeping law operations open and aboveboard, is a mild deterrent when authorities are catching and convicting lawbreakers, and 'proclaims the new methods of lawbreakers' thereby enabling public protection. List of harms: can show how to commit crime, give a false idea of crime prevalence, glamorize criminals, inform criminals of police strategy, 'try cases out of court' and warp juries, and subject law-abiding relatives to pitiless publicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain independence from police / avoid being a police apologist
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter's close contact with police can lead to lionizing them and presenting only the police version; the reporter must maintain independent judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate contacts but avoid becoming so afraid of offending officers that you become 'nothing but a police apologist.' Maintain tact and diplomacy to keep sources while preserving the right to independent judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six central police sources (know and use appropriately)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are probably six central sources of police information: the blotter, traffic bureau, detective bureau, other specialist divisions, 'private spikes,' and 'pipelines.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn how each source records and supplies information, what they can and cannot provide, and which to approach for details vs background. Each source has distinct limitations and uses (see individual entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blotter: use as public record but verify
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The blotter' records arrests with name, address and charge; it is usually a public document but gives too scanty information for good stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the blotter for the chronicle of routine day's events and to get names/charges; verify names/addresses and then talk to arresting officers for fuller details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traffic bureau records: verify accident details
rubrics_metrics.description: Traffic bureaus may record all accidents and often keep records of injured persons and extent of injuries, but these records 'cannot be accepted as authentic' because information is obtained under unfavorable circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always verify names, addresses, and statements describing mishaps by interviewing participants/witnesses; accident reports from traffic blotters require verification (discussed in following chapter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Detective bureau: provides 'news skeletons' not full stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Detective bureau records give skeletons — arrests will be recorded but the sleuthing that led to them will not be detailed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To learn the investigative sequence, 'talk to the detectives.' The bureau is a place for adroit listening and questioning rather than transcription of full stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialist divisions: know city specialties and where records are kept
rubrics_metrics.description: Other specialist divisions (arson squad, railroad detail, etc.) keep separate records and operate differently city to city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn which division to approach for details of a given case and which officers are in charge; know whether records are entered on general blotter, detective bureau, or kept separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private spikes / confidential records: access and printing limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Some officers keep 'private records' (e.g., detective bureau 'alibi book') that are not generally public but are often accessible to reporters; entries may be marked 'N. P.' ('Not for Publication').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These confidential sources provide background beyond official records; how freely to print such material 'is entirely a matter of the practices of the individual police department.' Ask about permissions and respect 'N. P.' markings and department policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pipelines: cultivate discreet informants
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Pipelines' are in-the-know officers who will tip the reporter to projected or in-process developments and fill in background when primary officers are unavailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop these informants by showing discretion, ability to protect sources, and steady intelligent judgment. Use them to amplify and clarify police action but avoid revealing identities; keep silent about information until the right time to disclose it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and constant verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy is obtained only with constant vigilance (example: verifying a name that is misreported in an initial officer's statement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify all factual details (names, addresses, statements). Perfunctory checks are insufficient — check directories, interview multiple sources, and double-check unexpected facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate the 'why' behind routine events
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Of the five Ws, the 'why' always must be investigated with utmost thoroughness' because routine transfers or shifts may reveal politics or policy changes of wider significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow up on routine items (transfers, beat changes, promotions) to uncover larger stories (e.g., reshuffles, policy changes) that can elevate a story to major pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cynicism and control emotional reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporter must learn to be suspicious but 'control this suspiciousness' so as not to become a cynic; also must 'control his emotions' to write accurate, dispassionate stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't let exposure to the worst aspects of human behavior harden you; maintain sensitiveness to human nature and the ability to report dispassionately even after hearing distressing accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resourcefulness within ethical limits
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of resourcefulness: unethical skullduggery (stealing photos, impersonating officers) which is nearly obsolete, and shrewd ingenuity within honor and honesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clever reporting devices that respect honesty and honor (phone calls from drugstores, cajoling reluctant sources) rather than deceit; the best rule of thumb is that ingenuity is justified only if it can be prefixed by 'honest' or 'honorable.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling suspects and naming conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A person is not a 'suspect' simply because brought to headquarters for questioning; when legally a suspect he is arrested on an 'open charge' allowing detention for a limited time. Material witnesses may be detained but are 'not prisoners.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful about naming: many papers omit names of those held on open charge because many are released; office policy usually decides exceptions. If police say a warrant 'will be issued,' exercise caution in using the name — when in doubt, don't name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain criminals' methods without instructing criminals
rubrics_metrics.description: Explaining methods used in a crime calls for skillful phrasing so the information helps the public protect itself rather than giving other criminals a how-to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid giving explicit, easily replicable details (example: instead of saying a burglar put 'anise seed' in cuffs, write 'certain materials whose smell attracts dogs'); when describing preventative measures, avoid wording that challenges criminals (example: rewrite overconfident alarm descriptions to avoid showing obvious weaknesses). Make small changes to keep information useful to the public but not useful to criminals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police version: present official record but beware police theorizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Official, documented information (name, charge, immediate disposition) is safe to print; police explanations, theorizings, and ramifications may be unprotected from libel and can be highly unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Print official records without fear; handle police speculation cautiously and balance it with the accused's account; do not rely solely on police argument as it lopsides the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique of fairness — story structure (Blocks 1–6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a six-block structure so that the accused's version is presented as prominently as the police account: Block 1 name/charge; Block 2 circumstances; Block 3 summary of police version; Block 4 summary of defendant's defense; Block 5 expansion of police view; Block 6 expansion of defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Putting Blocks 3 and 4 close together near the top signals to readers that there is another side; this reduces 'trying cases out of court' and allows headlines to reflect both sides. Even if police detail runs long, the early proximity of defense summary preserves fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with victims' identifications and named accusations
rubrics_metrics.description: Victims may be confident in naming 'who did it,' but their sureness may be mistaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not name the person a victim mentions until a warrant has been taken out, unless the person is already on a wanted list or the crime fits a known pattern. Err on the side of not naming when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept police blanket explanations for unsolved crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should resist the habit of letting police attribute unsolved crimes to 'outside professionals' as a way to justify failure to find the criminal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question such sweeping assertions and continue to pursue leads rather than dropping stories because police declare them the work of 'outside professionals.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Report on police brutality ('the third degree') with awareness of difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolonged, illegal, and sometimes torturous questioning ('third degree') occurs in some cities; it is outside the law and has sometimes been tolerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to and report such practices where they exist; recognize that few reporters have found satisfactory ways to deal with this, and that the practice can tarnish a city's reputation. Seek corroboration and be aware of human-rights/legal contexts when covering allegations of brutality.
